safety_line: Roaches can carry bacteria picked up outdoors. Wash hands after cleanup and keep food covered.
traits: Reddish-brown, 1.5-2 inches long, with a pale yellowish band behind the head
Can glide-fly, usually from a high spot toward light
Wanders in from mulch, palms, and drains, especially after heavy rain or drought
The largest common roach found in Florida homes

look_alikes.difference: American cockroaches have a pale band behind the head; smokybrown cockroaches are uniformly dark mahogany with no band.

copy.what_it_means: The classic Florida "palmetto bug" lives outdoors in mulch, palms, and sewers — one indoors is usually a visitor, not an infestation. Occasional wanderers are weather-driven; nightly sightings point to an entry point or moisture source worth fixing.
copy.fact: It lives outdoors in mulch, palms, and sewers — one in the house is a visitor, not necessarily an infestation.
copy.blurb: The classic Florida "palmetto bug" — a large outdoor roach that wanders inside from mulch, palms, and drains. Occasional sightings are usually weather-driven; frequent ones point to an entry point or moisture source worth checking.

tech_notes: Reddish, yellow pronotum band, strong flier. Source: mulch beds, palm boots, sewer/drain lines. Exterior-first program + dewebbing entry points.

safety_line: Roaches can carry bacteria picked up outdoors. Wash hands after cleanup and keep food covered.

traits: Uniform dark mahogany-to-black, no light band behind the head
About 1 to 1.25 inches, strong flier drawn to porch lights
Favors gutters, tree holes, and attics — needs consistent moisture
Wings extend past the abdomen in both sexes

look_alikes.difference: Smokybrown cockroaches are uniformly dark with no band behind the head; American cockroaches have a pale yellow band there.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up from above of the area right behind the head.

copy.what_it_means: Smokybrown cockroaches follow moisture, so clogged gutters and damp attics are a favorite address. Porch-light visitors are normal; regular attic activity is worth addressing.
copy.fact: It dries out easily, so it follows moisture — clogged gutters are a favorite address for this one.
copy.blurb: Dries out easily, so it follows moisture — clogged gutters are a favorite address.

tech_notes: Uniform dark mahogany, strong flier. Check gutters, soffit vents, attic moisture. Exterior perimeter + attic inspection if recurring.

safety_line: German roach infestations can trigger allergies and asthma and can adulterate food with feces and shed skins. Keep food sealed and surfaces clean while treatment is underway.
traits: Small, tan, with two dark parallel racing stripes behind the head
Found near appliances, under sinks, and in cabinet hinges
Rarely survives outdoors in Florida — arrives via bags, boxes, or used appliances
Seeing them in daylight often suggests a heavy, established population

look_alikes.difference: German cockroaches have two straight parallel stripes on the pronotum; brown-banded cockroaches have bands across the wings and a more mottled look.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from above on the stripe or band pattern.

copy.what_it_means: German roaches breed indoors — kitchens and bathrooms — and multiply fast with overlapping generations. A technician typically starts with an inspection to scope a cleanout approach suited to how far it's spread.
copy.fact: This species rarely lives outdoors in Florida — it arrives in bags, boxes, and used appliances. It's a hitchhiker, not a cleanliness verdict.
copy.blurb: German roaches breed indoors — kitchens and bathrooms — and multiply fast. Worth having looked at quickly; a technician scopes a cleanout after inspecting the extent.

tech_notes: Two pronotum stripes, nymphs banded. Gel bait + IGR cleanout, no repellents. Grade infestation level for cleanout scope — quote after inspection.

traits: Large, wide, dark reddish-brown to black roach, up to about 1.5 inches long
Only short wing pads, never full wings; adults cannot fly
Releases a strong, skunky odor when threatened or crushed
Found outdoors in mulch, woodpiles, palmetto thatch and under rotting logs, not usually deep inside a house

look_alikes.difference: Florida woods roach has only short wing pads and cannot fly; smokybrown cockroach has full, shiny wings and flies well
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, a zoomed photo from directly above showing whether the wings cover the abdomen or stop short.

safety_line: Releases a strong-smelling defensive spray if handled or crushed; wash hands after contact.

copy.what_it_means: A large, flightless outdoor roach common in mulch and landscaping around Southwest Florida homes. It rarely sets up indoors, so most sightings just call for less mulch and debris right against the foundation.
copy.fact: It is sometimes called the stink roach because it sprays a skunk-like defensive fluid when it feels threatened.

tech_notes: Peridomestic species; does not typically colonize indoors. Reduce harborage (mulch, woodpiles) against foundation; perimeter treatment per label if numbers are heavy.

traits: Large, reddish-brown roach similar in size to an American cockroach
Pale yellow stripe along the leading edge of each wing, near the head
Pale yellow band around the edge of the shield behind the head (pronotum)
Flies readily and is often found around outdoor plants and mulch as well as indoors

copy.what_it_means: A large, flying roach that behaves a lot like the American cockroach, moving between mulch, plants and the house. An occasional sighting outdoors is normal in Florida; a technician can evaluate if it's getting inside regularly, especially around door thresholds and vents.
copy.fact: Despite the name, it likely originated in Africa and simply picked up the 'Australian' name from where it was first described.

tech_notes: Confirm yellow wing stripe/pronotum band to rule out American cockroach. Perimeter and harborage treatment per label; check attic/soffit vents for entry points.

traits: Large reddish-brown roach, almost identical in size and color to an American cockroach
Short, blunt, stubby tail appendages (cerci) at the tip of the abdomen
Wings held flat and shorter relative to the body than an American cockroach's
Found in tree holes, mulch, attics and wall voids, especially in warmer, humid spots

safety_line: Can contaminate food and surfaces it crawls over; wash any exposed dishes or counters.

copy.what_it_means: A large roach that is easy to mistake for the American cockroach but tends to breed higher up, in attics, palm boots and wall voids, rather than mostly at ground level. Worth treating like any other large roach problem.
copy.fact: It prefers to glue its egg case out of sight in a hidden crevice rather than carrying it around, which is one reason infestations can go unnoticed for a while.

tech_notes: Confirm via short/stubby cerci vs American cockroach's long cerci. Check attics, palm boots and upper wall voids in addition to usual ground-level harborage; treat per label.

traits: Small, light brown roach with two dark stripes behind the head, nearly identical to a German cockroach
Flies readily and strongly, often bursting into flight when disturbed
Drawn to lights at dusk and often seen swarming around porch lights or windows from outside
Lives mainly in mulch, thatch and leaf litter rather than setting up long-term indoor colonies

look_alikes.difference: Asian cockroach flies readily and is drawn outdoors to light at dusk; German cockroach looks nearly identical but rarely flies and stays hidden indoors
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, take a short video showing whether it takes flight when approached.

copy.what_it_means: A strong-flying lawn roach that swarms toward outdoor lights at dusk and can look just like a German cockroach, but it lives in the grass and mulch rather than nesting inside. Reducing outdoor lighting and treating the yard usually help more than spraying indoors.
copy.fact: It looks almost identical to the German cockroach, but flight is the tell — this one flies readily and the German cockroach almost never does.

tech_notes: Behavioral ID (flight, outdoor light attraction) is the practical way to separate from B. germanica since they look nearly identical. Focus treatment on lawn/mulch harborage and exterior lighting fixtures rather than indoor voids.

traits: Small tan to dark brown roach with two light bands crossing the wings and abdomen
Males have wings longer than the body and a more slender look than females
Prefers warm, dry spots up high, like inside cabinets, behind picture frames and inside electronics
Rarely found near sinks or drains, unlike most other indoor roaches

look_alikes.difference: Brown-banded has two pale crossbands and stays up high in dry areas; German cockroach has two dark stripes behind the head and stays low near water
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in from above showing whether the pale marks are crossbands on the wings or stripes behind the head.

safety_line: Can contaminate food and surfaces it crawls over; wash any exposed dishes or counters.

copy.what_it_means: A small roach that spreads out through a home instead of staying near the kitchen sink, so it often turns up in bedrooms, closets and behind picture frames. It breeds indoors year-round, so it's worth treating like any established roach problem.
copy.fact: Unlike most household roaches, it can thrive in dry rooms far from water because it gets enough moisture from the food it eats.

tech_notes: Check up high (cabinets, picture frames, electronics, closets) as well as usual low harborage; egg cases are often glued to hidden surfaces away from the ootheca-carrying female. Treat per label.

traits: Small, shiny, dark brown to black roach with pale tan wings that leave the tip of the head visible
Burrows a few inches into loose soil, mulch, compost and lawn thatch rather than hiding under debris
Feeds on plant roots and can wilt or damage container plants and garden beds
Almost never found deep indoors; stays in soil, mulch and potted plants

copy.what_it_means: A burrowing roach that lives in mulch, compost and potted plant soil and feeds on roots, which can stress container plants and garden beds. It's a yard and garden nuisance rather than a home-invading pest.
copy.fact: Nearly all Surinam cockroaches are female; the species reproduces largely by cloning itself without needing to mate.

tech_notes: Check potted plant soil and mulch beds for burrowing damage on ornamentals. Reduce mulch depth/moisture; perimeter or bed treatment per label if damaging valued plants.

traits: Pale green to yellow-green roach, unlike any other common Florida roach color
Strong flier, often seen at night circling porch lights or landing on screens
Adults are small and delicate-looking with a thin yellow line along the body edges
Rarely found indoors and does not form indoor colonies

copy.what_it_means: A harmless-looking, pale green roach that lives in trees, shrubs and leaf litter and only shows up around porch lights at night. It isn't known to bite, doesn't go after indoor food, and isn't worth treating on its own.
copy.fact: Its pale green color and habit of hitchhiking on fruit shipments from the Caribbean are how it earned the nickname banana roach.

tech_notes: Outdoor, light-attracted species; does not establish indoor infestations. No treatment typically warranted beyond reducing unnecessary exterior lighting if it is a nuisance.

traits: Droppings look like coarse ground pepper or small dark smears, often streaked along edges where roaches travel
Egg cases (oothecae) are hard, purse- or bean-shaped capsules with a ridged seam along one edge
Found clustered in cabinet corners, behind appliances, under sinks and along baseboards
A strong, musty, oily smell in a cabinet or pantry often shows up alongside heavier droppings

look_alikes.difference: Roach droppings vary in size and are often smeared or mixed with irregular egg cases; drywood termite pellets are uniform, ridged ovals with no smearing
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the pile showing whether the pieces are uniform in shape or mixed and smeared.

look_alikes.difference: Roach droppings show up in cabinets and along baseboards; bed bug signs (dark spotting, shed skins) cluster on mattress seams and bed frames
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the mattress seam or bed frame instead of the kitchen or pantry area.

safety_line: Wipe down and disinfect any surfaces where droppings or egg cases are found before storing food or dishes there again.

copy.what_it_means: Droppings and egg cases suggest roaches are breeding nearby rather than just passing through, though the amount and spread are what actually confirm that. Finding them in a kitchen or bathroom is a good reason to have it looked at even without spotting a live roach.
copy.fact: A single egg case can hold dozens of roach eggs, which is why droppings and cases turning up together often point to an established population.

tech_notes: Note distribution (kitchen/bath vs bedroom/closet) to help narrow likely species before treatment. Clean thoroughly and treat harborage per label; heavy droppings suggest an established population, not an occasional wanderer.
